analysis.one_liner: Bars new mining on about one million acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon.
analysis.headline: The bill to withdraw roughly 1,068,908 acres near the Grand Canyon from mining never reached a House vote; it died in committee after one hearing, leaving the land open to new mining claims.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed about 1,068,908 acres of federal land — the Tusayan Ranger District and land near Kanab Creek and House Rock Valley — from all new mining claims, mineral leasing, geothermal leasing, and mineral materials sales [S2] [S3]. The goal was to keep uranium and other mining out of the watersheds draining into the Grand Canyon and the Colorado River. It was introduced in January 2009, referred to the Natural Resources Committee and two of its subcommittees, got one hearing in July 2009, and never received a committee or floor vote before that Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink and use water from the Colorado River basin, downstream communities, and visitors to the Grand Canyon would gain protection of the watersheds from new uranium and hardrock mining, with the risks of contaminated runoff and long-term cleanup those operations can leave behind. Tribes and local communities concerned about mining activity near the canyon would also benefit. Existing mining rights are honored, so only new claims are affected [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Colorado River water users and the region

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws approximately 1,068,908 acres from location, entry, and patent under the mining laws, meaning no new mining claims could be staked on the land [S2] [S3].
Also withdraws the land from mineral leasing, geothermal leasing, and mineral materials laws, closing other avenues of extractive development [S2] [S3].
Protects the watersheds around the Grand Canyon from new mining activity and the water contamination risks it can create, while respecting valid existing mining rights [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies that would otherwise have been able to stake new claims, and obtain mineral or geothermal leases, on roughly one million acres near the Grand Canyon. Anyone hoping for mineral development jobs and royalties from those lands also forgoes that opportunity. Holders of valid existing rights keep their claims [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal is subject to valid existing rights, so mining operations with already-established claims could continue, limiting the bill's actual protective reach [S2] [S3].

Withdrawing about a million acres from all entry, disposal, mining, and leasing forecloses mineral development on that land, forgoing potential jobs, royalties, and domestic mineral supply — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is permanent watershed protection for a national icon and a major water supply against forgone mineral development on the affected acres. The bill was drafted to spare existing claim holders, so the cost falls mainly on future mining activity. Whether the protection is worth the forgone development is a genuine judgment call, but the water-supply and Grand Canyon values at stake are the stated reason the bill drew 50 cosponsors [S2] [S4].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees for nearly two years, got a single hearing, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on January 22, 2009, with Reps. Hinchey, Rahall, and Pastor as original cosponsors [S1] [S5].

The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and on February 4, 2009, to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
The subcommittees held a hearing on July 21, 2009, the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup or a vote in the House or Senate, and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].
It had 50 cosponsors — 49 House Democrats and one House Republican — but that support never translated into floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies came out ahead: because the bill died, the roughly one million acres near the Grand Canyon remained open to new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing under existing law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies keeping access to the land

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva

for.name: 49 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad Democratic House support.

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor whose committee held a subcommittee hearing on the bill in July 2009 but never brought it to a committee or floor vote.

for.name: Rep. Ed Pastor

against.name: Natural Resources Committee leadership

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote on the bill, leaving it to expire without floor action.

against.name: Uranium mining industry
against.role: Opponents of Grand Canyon-area mining withdrawals
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed withdrawing federal land around the Grand Canyon from new mining claims, arguing the area held significant uranium reserves.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 49 of 253 House Democrats and just 1 of 178 House Republicans — and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would have barred new mining claims and leases on about one million acres near the Grand Canyon, land the industry valued for uranium. Its gain from the bill's death was continued access to that public land, while the public bears the water-contamination risk mining there can create.
The withdrawal also closed the land to geothermal leasing and mineral materials sales, blocking development those interests could otherwise pursue.
